summary: This standards-track document defines the Network Management Datastore Architecture, a framework for datastores that connects YANG data models to protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF. It builds on experience with earlier approaches and separates configuration that is intended from the state a device is actually using. It is the basis for other YANG models written to be NMDA-compatible.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8342 defines common places for network devices to store and report configuration and operational state. It lets a model describe a data item once while showing both the requested value and the value the device is using.

subtitle: A common datastore model separates intended configuration from the state a device is using.

tldr.problem: The earlier YANG model often described configuration and operational state in separate schema branches, duplicating definitions and making their relationship hard for software to interpret.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8342 defines conceptual datastores for configuration and operational state. A data object can be defined once and have separate values in those datastores, with origin metadata identifying configuration sources.
tldr.outcome: It provides a protocol-independent datastore architecture and updates RFC 7950. RFC 8342 has itself been updated by RFC 8808 and RFC 10016.

today: RFC 8342 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7950. It has been updated by RFC 8808 and RFC 10016.

sections.title: Why the Datastore Model Changed
sections.content:
A network setting can have one value that an operator configured and another value that the device is actually using. The values may differ because of hardware, protocol interactions, processing delays, or configuration transformations.

The earlier approach often represented configuration and state in separate branches of a YANG model. That duplicated definitions, made models harder to read, and did not make the relationship between the branches easy for software to follow. RFC 8342 instead lets one schema definition have independent instances in different datastores.

This design also supports systems that transform configuration, such as removing inactive entries or expanding templates, before applying it.
sections.plainLanguage: A requested setting and the value in use can differ. The architecture describes the setting once and lets separate datastores show each value.

sections.title: Configuration Datastores
sections.content:
A datastore is a conceptual place to store and access information, represented as an instantiated YANG data tree. The conventional configuration datastores share a schema, so protocols can copy data between them. The architecture identifies these datastores without requiring every management protocol to expose all of them.

  • <running> holds the device's current configuration and must be a valid configuration tree.
  • <candidate> can be edited without changing the current configuration, then committed to <running>.
  • <startup> holds configuration loaded at boot on devices that keep it separate.
  • <intended> is read-only and holds <running> after transformations. It is the configuration the system attempts to apply.

When <running> changes, a server must immediately update and validate <intended>. In a simple implementation, they can be identical.
sections.plainLanguage: The configuration datastores hold different stages of a device's settings. The read-only <intended> datastore shows the transformed settings the device is trying to apply.

sections.title: Dynamic and Operational Data
sections.content:
A dynamic configuration datastore holds settings obtained while the device is running through interaction with other systems. This data is not part of persistent configuration and is lost on reboot. Its schema may differ from the conventional configuration schema.

The read-only <operational> datastore combines system state with configuration actually in use. It can include applied values from <intended>, dynamic, learned, and system-provided configuration, and model defaults. A missing node means the device is not using that value.

Configuration for a resource that is unavailable can remain in <intended> without appearing in <operational>. When resources change, old configuration may remain operational until the system releases the resources it used.
sections.plainLanguage: The operational datastore reports values the device is using, along with its changing state. A requested setting for a resource that is missing can remain intended without being reported as in use.

sections.title: The Origin of Configuration Values
sections.content:
The architecture defines an origin metadata annotation for configuration in <operational>. Its values identify whether configuration came from the intended datastore, a dynamic datastore, the system, another protocol or system, a model default, or an unknown source.

The origin applies to configuration nodes, with child nodes inheriting the annotation from a parent when they do not have their own. Devices should report the source that best describes the value in use. If the source cannot be determined, the device should report unknown.

When equal values could have come from different sources, the YANG description should guide the choice. For example, a protocol-negotiated value that overrides configured data is marked as learned even if both values happen to match.
sections.plainLanguage: Each configuration value in the operational datastore can say where it came from. If the device cannot identify the source, it can mark the origin as unknown.

sections.title: Changes to YANG Processing
sections.content:
RFC 8342 updates RFC 7950 by refining the accessible data tree used in some XPath expressions. Expressions associated with system state, notifications, and RPC or action input and output use operational state in the server as part of their context.

Actions run in the context of the operational datastore, and the node on which an action is invoked must exist there. The RFC does not restrict what an RPC or action may do, so an operation may still modify a datastore.
sections.plainLanguage: Some YANG rules and actions now use the operational datastore as their view of the device. An action can run only on a node that exists in that view.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says its datastore architecture has no security impact on the Internet. The YANG modules it defines contain identities and a metadata annotation.

The origin annotation may reveal which control-plane protocols are active. It is available only to clients allowed to read the applied configuration, and administrators should consider its sensitivity when setting access controls.
sections.plainLanguage: Origin information can reveal clues about how a device is operating. Administrators should limit access to it as they do for the applied configuration it describes.
